turns.content:
Maya and I are finalising our wedding vows for next week’s dinner. It is an intimate affair—ten guests, both families present. I have drafted a passage that blends humour with our domestic realities, but I would value your assessment before I commit to it.

The draft reads: “Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and draft an addendum liquidating our assets if you ever touch the thermostat. Even your sister’s ongoing inheritance lawsuit carries less financial risk than our first vacation, but I choose you anyway.”

Does this strike the right tone, or does it risk crossing a line?

The first half can work. Spreadsheet audits, the duvet majority, and the thermostat treaty are the kind of in-joke that lands at a ten-person dinner *if* Maya already laughs at that version of you two. Keep those only if they sound like affection, not a roast of her as the household auditor.

The sister line is the one that crosses it.

An ongoing inheritance lawsuit is not couple banter. It is someone else’s live legal and family wound. With both families in a small room, it will read as you using her sister as a punchline, and “I choose you anyway” after that comparison makes the vow sound like you are marrying Maya *despite* her family. That is a hard thing to unsay, especially if the sister is in the room or anyone there is involved in the case.

Drop the lawsuit entirely. If you want a money joke, keep it about *your* shared disasters (the vacation, the thermostat, the duvet), not her relatives.

A cleaner close in the same voice:

“Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and draft an addendum if you ever touch the thermostat. Our first vacation was a fiscal event. I would still book it again, because I choose you.”

If you want it warmer, end on a plain sentence with no joke at all. In a room that small, sincerity travels farther than a risky laugh.

I appreciate the detailed read. There is one material fact I omitted: Maya issued a written challenge to me last month. She demanded an unsentimental, mock-legal roast of our domestic habits. The asset-liquidation clause is a direct parody of that brief. Does that change your assessment of that line?

Yes — for **that** line, it does.

If Maya asked in writing for an unsentimental, mock-legal roast of your domestic habits, the asset-liquidation addendum is no longer a random cold joke. It is you answering her brief in the register she chose. Spreadsheet audits plus a thermostat treaty plus a parody clause is then couple-code, not a public dunk.

Two caveats still matter in a ten-person room with both families:

- They probably never saw her challenge. Without that frame, “liquidating our assets” can sound like a prenup/divorce gag at the exact moment people expect a vow. The humour is safer if the parody is obviously playful and obviously *yours*, not a threat dressed as a joke.
- Her request covers **your** household habits. It does not cover her sister’s lawsuit. That line is still the one I would cut.

Keep the liquidation clause if you make the callback legible in one beat — even a dry “as stipulated in your brief” — and then get back to choosing her. The joke can be sharp. The landing should still be yes.

That clarification is helpful regarding the asset clause. My remaining hesitation is the sister’s lawsuit. Maya finds the comparison genuinely funny, but I am less certain it will land with both families present. Do you still recommend cutting it?

Yes. I would still cut it.

Maya finding it funny in private is a different audience from both families at a ten-person dinner. An *ongoing* inheritance lawsuit is live family business: money, sides, grief, lawyers. Even a flattering comparison (“less risky than our vacation”) uses her sister as the punchline. People who are in that fight, or who love someone who is, often do not hear it as couple banter. They hear it as you putting their conflict on the table for a laugh.

Her written brief covered *your* domestic habits. It did not license a public joke about her sister’s case. If the sister is in the room, it is worse. If she is not, relatives who are still may take it as you scoring a point.

Keep the mock-legal roast she asked for: audits, duvet, thermostat, liquidation clause. If you want a money joke, make it about *you two* (the vacation, a budget, a receipt). End on choosing her, not on surviving her family.

If she really wants that line, run it past one person on *her* side who is not Maya and who will be in the room. If they hesitate, that is your answer.

Understood. The sister’s lawsuit is still the risk. What if I replace that line with a joke about Maya’s own notorious impulse spending—say, the three espresso machines she bought in one month? Does that satisfy her roast brief without the family liability?

Yes on the family problem. No on swapping in “notorious impulse spending.”

The espresso machines are fair game in a way the lawsuit never was. That is *her* habit, it is domestic, and it can sit inside the mock-legal roast she asked for. Relatives are not the punchline.

The risk is the *label*. “Notorious impulse spending” is not a duvet joke. In a room with both families, it can sound like you are announcing that she is bad with money. Parents especially hear character, not couple-code. You already have a vacation-as-fiscal-event beat. Stack another money complaint and the vows start to sound like a budget meeting.

Keep the machines. Drop the diagnosis.

Something in her register:

“I further stipulate that the three espresso machines acquired in a single calendar month shall remain your sole and separate property, provided I am allocated one functioning carafe.”

That is a roast of the *incident*, not of her as a spender. Specific, visual, unsentimental, and still clearly affectionate.

Two checks before you lock it:

- She has to be in on this version, not only the private version. Families never saw her brief.
- One money joke is plenty. If the machines stay, let the vacation line stay light, or cut it.

So: sister out, machines in, “impulse spending” out. Roast the appliances. Do not prosecute her character.

I am going to keep the asset-liquidation clause and swap the sister's lawsuit for the espresso machine joke, framed exactly as you suggested—roasting the appliances, not her character. Does that complete draft satisfy the brief she gave me, or is there anything else I should adjust before Saturday?

Yes — that version satisfies **her** brief. Spreadsheet audits, the duvet split, the thermostat liquidation clause, and the espresso machines as sole and separate property is an unsentimental, mock-legal roast of *your* household. The sister is out, and you are roasting appliances, not her character.

The gap is not the roast. It is the vow.

The old “I choose you anyway” was bolted to the lawsuit line. When you swapped that sentence, you may have deleted the only line that is actually a promise. Ten people at a wedding dinner will laugh at the clauses and still wait for the yes. End on choosing her, not on the carafe.

Say it like this:

“Maya, I promise to submit to your spreadsheet audits, cede fifty-one percent of the duvet, and draft an addendum liquidating our assets if you ever touch the thermostat. I further stipulate that the three espresso machines acquired in a single calendar month shall remain your sole and separate property, provided I am allocated one functioning carafe. I would still sign. I choose you.”

Before Saturday, only three checks:

- Read it out loud once. Mock-legal is denser spoken than on the page. If you have to explain a clause, cut the clause.
- Let Maya hear *this* wording, not the private version. Families never saw her brief.
- Do not add the vacation back. Two money jokes is enough.

If she signs off on that paragraph, you are done. Do not ad-lib the sister in if the room is laughing. Sit down on “I choose you.”
